question.prompt: An \(11\times11\times11\) wooden cube is formed by gluing together \(11^3\) unit cubes. What is the greatest number of unit cubes that can be seen from a single point?

solutions.explanation:
From a single exterior point, at most one face from each opposite pair can face the observer. Every visible unit cube must belong to one of these observer-facing outer face layers, so at most three adjacent face layers contribute. Looking from above, in front of, and to the right of the cube shows all three corresponding faces. Thus we can attain the maximum by counting the cubes on these three faces.

Count them in an order that avoids repetition. The front face contains \(11\cdot11=121\) cubes. The right face adds \(11\cdot10=110\) cubes, because its column along the front edge was already counted. On the top face, omit the front row and the right column, leaving \(10\cdot10=100\) new cubes.

Each cube on the three faces is counted on its first face in this order, so none is missed or counted twice. The maximum is
\[
121+110+100=331,
\]
choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
solutions.title: Count new cubes face by face

solutions.explanation:
Only one face from each pair of opposite faces can face an exterior observer, so visible cubes lie on at most three adjacent outer face layers. Any smaller selection is contained in such a three-face selection. A viewpoint beyond their common corner shows all three faces, so their union gives the greatest possible count.

Each face contains \(11^2=121\) unit cubes, giving an initial count of \(3\cdot121\). Each pair of faces shares a row of \(11\) cubes along its common edge. Subtract these three shared rows to correct the repeated counts.

The single cube at the common corner was initially counted three times and then subtracted three times. Add it back once. All other cubes now have count one, so the number of distinct visible cubes is
\[
3\cdot121-3\cdot11+1=331.
\]
The answer is \(331\), choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
